claim: Prostate cancer is the most frequent cancer in men.
source: Prostate is the most frequent cancer in men.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, citing Center et al., 2012

claim: Prostate cancer progression is driven by androgen steroid hormones.
source: Prostate cancer progression is driven by androgen steroid hormones, and delayed by androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge

claim: Prostate cancer progression is delayed by androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
source: Prostate cancer progression is driven by androgen steroid hormones, and delayed by androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge

claim: Androgens control transcription by stimulating androgen receptor (AR) activity.
source: Androgens control transcription by stimulating androgen receptor (AR) activity, yet also control pre-mRNA splicing through less clear mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge

claim: Androgens control pre-mRNA splicing through less clear mechanisms.
source: Androgens control transcription by stimulating androgen receptor (AR) activity, yet also control pre-mRNA splicing through less clear mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap

claim: Androgens regulate splicing through AR-mediated transcriptional control of ESRP2.
source: Here we find androgens regulate splicing through AR-mediated transcriptional control of the epithelial-specific splicing regulator ESRP2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including ChIP, qPCR, and Western blot analyses shown in Figure 1

claim: ESRP2 is highly expressed in primary prostate cancer.
source: Both ESRP2 and its close paralog ESRP1 are highly expressed in primary prostate cancer.
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis of 719 clinical prostate cancer tumours and experimental validation shown in Figure 2

claim: ESRP1 is highly expressed in primary prostate cancer.
source: Both ESRP2 and its close paralog ESRP1 are highly expressed in primary prostate cancer.
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis of 719 clinical prostate cancer tumours and experimental validation shown in Figure 2

claim: Androgen stimulation induces splicing switches in many endogenous ESRP2-controlled mRNA isoforms.
source: Androgen stimulation induces splicing switches in many endogenous ESRP2-controlled mRNA isoforms, including splicing switches correlating with disease progression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR analysis of splicing patterns shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Some ESRP2-controlled splicing switches correlate with disease progression.
source: Androgen stimulation induces splicing switches in many endogenous ESRP2-controlled mRNA isoforms, including splicing switches correlating with disease progression.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data shown in Figure 5

claim: ESRP2 expression in clinical prostate cancer is repressed by ADT.
source: ESRP2 expression in clinical prostate cancer is repressed by ADT, which may thus inadvertently dampen epithelial splice programmes.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data from human prostate cancer pre- and post-ADT shown in Figure 1A

claim: ADT may inadvertently dampen epithelial splice programmes.
source: ESRP2 expression in clinical prostate cancer is repressed by ADT, which may thus inadvertently dampen epithelial splice programmes.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that ESRP2 is repressed by ADT and ESRP2 controls epithelial splicing patterns

claim: Treatment with the AR antagonist bicalutamide (Casodex) induced mesenchymal splicing patterns of genes including FLNB and CTNND1.
source: Supporting this, treatment with the AR antagonist bicalutamide (Casodex) induced mesenchymal splicing patterns of genes including FLNB and CTNND1.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: ESRP2 expression decreased following ADT in 7/7 prostate cancer patients.
source: ESRP2 expression decreased following ADT in 7/7 prostate cancer patients (Rajan et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of RNAseq data from patients and shown in Figure 1A

claim: RNAseq data from LTL331 patient-derived xenografts showed reduced ESRP2 mRNA levels following castration and relapse neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC).
source: Furthermore, RNAseq data prepared from different stages of LTL331 patient-derived xenografts (Akamatsu et al., 2015) showed reduced ESRP2 mRNA levels following castration and relapse neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: ESRP1 expression levels reduced following ADT.
source: ESRP1 expression levels also reduced following ADT (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: ESRP1 showed less change in gene expression compared to ESRP2 in patient-derived xenografts following castration or relapse NEPC.
source: However, ESRP1 showed less change in gene expression compared to ESRP2 in patient-derived xenografts following castration or relapse NEPC (Figure 1C) (Akamatsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNAseq data shown in Figures 1B and 1C

claim: High endogenous levels of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 proteins are detected within the AR positive LNCaP and CWR22 RV1 prostate cancer cell lines.
source: Western blots detected high endogenous levels of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 proteins within the AR positive LNCaP and CWR22 RV1 prostate cancer cell lines, as compared to the AR negative PC3 and DU145 prostate cancer cell lines (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 1D and 1E

claim: AR negative PC3 and DU145 prostate cancer cell lines have lower levels of ESRP1 and ESRP2 proteins compared to AR positive cell lines.
source: Western blots detected high endogenous levels of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 proteins within the AR positive LNCaP and CWR22 RV1 prostate cancer cell lines, as compared to the AR negative PC3 and DU145 prostate cancer cell lines (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 1D and 1E

claim: Androgens activated ESRP2 gene expression in AR-positive LNCaP cells.
source: However, qPCR analysis showed that while androgens activated ESRP2 gene expression in response to in AR-positive LNCaP cells, this was not observed for ESRP1 gene expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Androgens did not activate ESRP1 gene expression in AR-positive LNCaP cells.
source: However, qPCR analysis showed that while androgens activated ESRP2 gene expression in response to in AR-positive LNCaP cells, this was not observed for ESRP1 gene expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Androgen mediated-control of ESRP2 expression was detected in VCaP and RWPE-1 AR-expressing prostate cell lines.
source: Androgen mediated-control of ESRP2 expression was also detected in two additional AR-expressing prostate cell lines (VCaP and RWPE-1, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G

claim: ESRP2 protein expression was detected 48 hr after androgen exposure.
source: ESRP2 protein expression was detected 48 hr after androgen exposure, with ESRP1 protein levels not changing over this same time-period (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H

claim: ESRP1 protein levels did not change over 48 hr after androgen exposure.
source: ESRP2 protein expression was detected 48 hr after androgen exposure, with ESRP1 protein levels not changing over this same time-period (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H

claim: ESRP2 gene expression in LNCaP cells was rapidly induced in response to 10 nM of R1881.
source: ESRP2 gene expression in LNCaP cells was rapidly induced in response to 10 nM of the synthetic androgen analogue R1881 (methytrienolone) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by time course qPCR data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation from LNCaP cells confirmed direct AR binding to a site within 20 Kb of the ESRP2 gene promoter.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) from LNCaP cells confirmed direct AR binding to a site within 20 Kb of the ESRP2 gene promoter that had been previously predicted from a genome-wide study (at position chr16: 68210834–68211293 on human genome assembly hg38) (Massie et al., 2011) (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1J

claim: ESRP2 transcription in LNCaP cells was induced over a wide range of R1881 concentrations, ranging from 1 nM to 100 nM.
source: Consistent with ESRP2 regulation at physiological androgen concentrations, ESRP2 transcription in LNCaP cells was induced over a wide range of R1881 concentrations, ranging from 1 nM to 100 nM (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1K

claim: Meta-analysis of 719 clinical prostate cancer tumours from 11 previously published studies detected significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 in 9/11 datasets.
source: Meta-analysis of 719 clinical prostate cancer tumours from 11 previously published studies detected significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 in 9/11 datasets (Figure 2—source data 1) (Arredouani et al., 2009; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2015; Fraser et al., 2017; Grasso et al., 2012; Lapointe et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2010; Tomlins et al., 2007; Vanaja et al., 2003; Varambally et al., 2005; Wallace et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis of published datasets

claim: Real-time PCR showed significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 mRNA in prostate carcinoma relative to benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH).
source: Real-time PCR showed significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 mRNA in (1) prostate carcinoma relative to benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) (Figure 2A); and (2) in nine prostate tumour samples relative to matched normal tissue from the same patient (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Real-time PCR showed significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 mRNA in nine prostate tumour samples relative to matched normal tissue from the same patient.
source: Real-time PCR showed significant up-regulation of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 mRNA in (1) prostate carcinoma relative to benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) (Figure 2A); and (2) in nine prostate tumour samples relative to matched normal tissue from the same patient (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: ESRP1 was 2.76 fold up-regulated in the 'metastatic-subgroup' compared to the 'non-metastatic subgroup' in the Walker et al. (2017) study.
source: A recent study by Walker et al. (2017) identified a molecular subgroup of prostate cancers with metastatic potential at presentation. Within this dataset ESRP1 was 2.76 fold up-regulated in the 'metastatic-subgroup' compared to the 'non-metastatic subgroup'.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published data from Walker et al. (2017)

claim: ESRP1 gene expression was significantly upregulated in primary prostate cancer patients presenting with a metastatic biology.
source: Using RNA from a subset of samples from the Walker et al. study, we confirmed significant (p<0.05) upregulation of the ESRP1 gene in primary prostate cancer patients presenting with a metastatic biology (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: ESRP2 gene expression did not significantly increase in the 20 samples studied from the Walker et al. cohort.
source: ESRP2 gene expression did not significantly increase in the 20 samples studied.
evidence: This is based on analysis of samples from the Walker et al. cohort

claim: Levels of E-Cadherin were not significantly increased between BPH compared to prostate carcinoma.
source: Arguing against this possibility, levels of E-Cadherin were not significantly increased between BPH compared to prostate carcinoma, or between matched tumour and normal prostate tissue from patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Levels of E-Cadherin were not significantly increased between matched tumour and normal prostate tissue from patients.
source: Arguing against this possibility, levels of E-Cadherin were not significantly increased between BPH compared to prostate carcinoma, or between matched tumour and normal prostate tissue from patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: High ESRP1 expression associated with a significantly reduced time to first biochemical recurrence (p=0.022) in the TCGA PRAD cohort.
source: High ESRP2 expression was not prognostic of disease progression in the TCGA (PRostate ADenocarcinoma) PRAD cohort analysed using KM-express (Chen et al., 2018), but high expression of ESRP1 associated with a significantly reduced time to first biochemical recurrence (p=0.022) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 2D

claim: High ESRP2 expression was not prognostic of disease progression in the TCGA PRAD cohort.
source: High ESRP2 expression was not prognostic of disease progression in the TCGA (PRostate ADenocarcinoma) PRAD cohort analysed using KM-express (Chen et al., 2018), but high expression of ESRP1 associated with a significantly reduced time to first biochemical recurrence (p=0.022) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA data using KM-express

claim: Ectopic expression of ESRP1 and ESRP2 protein expression in AR negative PC3 and DU145 cell line models reduced prostate cancer cell growth in vitro.
source: Ectopic expression of ESRP1 and ESRP2 protein expression in AR negative PC3 and DU145 cell line models reduced prostate cancer cell growth in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Over-expression of ESRP1 in PC3 cells significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo.
source: Over-expression of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 (either alone or together) in PC3 cells also significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Over-expression of ESRP2 in PC3 cells significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo.
source: Over-expression of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 (either alone or together) in PC3 cells also significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Over-expression of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 together in PC3 cells significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo.
source: Over-expression of both ESRP1 and ESRP2 (either alone or together) in PC3 cells also significantly slowed growth of prostate cancer xenografts in vivo (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Bioinformatic analysis predicted 446 ESRP1/ESRP2 regulated alternative splicing events across 319 genes (ΔPSI > 10%, p<0.05).
source: Bioinformatic analysis (Trincado et al., 2018) of these RNAseq data (GSE129540) predicted 446 ESRP1/ESRP2 regulated alternative splicing events across 319 genes (ΔPSI > 10%, p<0.05) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of RNAseq data using SUPPA2

claim: 44 predicted ESRP1/ESRP2-controlled exons were experimentally validated by RT-PCR analysis.
source: We experimentally validated splicing switches for 44 predicted ESRP1/ESRP2-controlled exons by RT-PCR analysis, after LNCaP cells were treated with either of two independent sets of siRNAs directed against ESRP1 and ESRP2 or control siRNAs (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 3

claim: Similar splicing switches were detected for 35/44 of these skipped exons after jointly depleting ESRP1 and 2 from the AR-positive CWR22 RV1 prostate cancer cell line.
source: We detected similar splicing switches for 35/44 of these skipped exons after jointly depleting ESRP1 and 2 from the AR-positive CWR22 RV1 prostate cancer cell line.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from CWR22 RV1 cells shown in Figure 3

claim: 28/44 of these splicing switches were observed after jointly depleting ESRP1 and ESRP2 from the AR positive PNT2 cells.
source: 28/44 of these splicing switches were also observed after jointly depleting ESRP1 and ESRP2 from the AR positive PNT2 cells that model the normal prostate epithelium (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from PNT2 cells shown in Figure 3

claim: Ectopic expression of either ESRP1 or ESRP2 in PC3 cells induced splicing switches for 31/42 exons analysed.
source: Ectopic expression of either ESRP1 or ESRP2 in PC3 cells induced splicing switches for 31/42 exons analysed.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR analysis of PC3 cells with ectopic ESRP expression shown in Figure 3

claim: The splicing switches induced by ectopic expression of either ESRP2 or ESRP1 were reciprocal to the splicing switches detected after siRNA depletion of ESRP1/ESRP2.
source: Importantly, the splicing switches induced by ectopic expression of either ESRP2 or ESRP1 were reciprocal to the splicing switches detected after siRNA depletion of ESRP1/ESRP2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: More than 70% (37/44) exons in the test panel demonstrated androgen regulated splicing.
source: Consistent with these expectations, more than 70% (37/44) exons in our test panel demonstrated androgen regulated splicing (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR analysis of LNCaP cells treated with androgens

claim: Plotting the PSI for each exon after 48 hr androgen stimulation versus the PSI after ESRP1/ESRP2 depletion showed a significant negative correlation (slope = −0.66, R2 = 0.64, p<0.0001).
source: Importantly, plotting the percent spliced-in (PSI) for each exon after 48 hr androgen stimulation (Y axis) versus the PSI after ESRP1/ESRP2 depletion (X axis) showed a significant negative correlation (slope = −0.66, R2 = 0.64, p<0.0001) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Exons that showed more exon skipping in response to ESRP1/ESRP2 depletion had higher splicing inclusion after androgen stimulation.
source: Thus, exons that showed more exon skipping in response to ESRP1/ESRP2 depletion had higher splicing inclusion after androgen stimulation (which would induce ESRP2 expression) (examples shown in Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation shown in Figure 4A and examples in Figure 4B

claim: Exons that showed higher splicing inclusion in response to ESRP1/2 depletion had less splicing inclusion after androgen stimulation.
source: Reciprocally, exons that showed higher splicing inclusion in response to ESRP1/2 depletion also had less splicing inclusion after androgen stimulation (examples shown in Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation shown in Figure 4A and examples in Figure 4C

claim: 19/38 ESRP-regulated exons have different patterns of splicing inclusion between tumour and normal tissue in the PRAD cohort.
source: Further analysis of the PRAD cohort revealed that 19/38 ESRP-regulated exons also have different patterns of splicing inclusion between tumour and normal tissue (Figure 5E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data shown in Figure 5E

claim: DOCK7 exon 23 is excluded more frequently in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue.
source: These differentially spliced exons include the AR-ESRP2-controlled alternative exons in the DOCK7 and RPS24 genes (both of which were excluded in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue); and the alternative exons in the MINK1 and MAP3K7 genes (each of which had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data

claim: RPS24 exon 5 is excluded more frequently in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue.
source: These differentially spliced exons include the AR-ESRP2-controlled alternative exons in the DOCK7 and RPS24 genes (both of which were excluded in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue); and the alternative exons in the MINK1 and MAP3K7 genes (each of which had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data

claim: MINK1 alternative exons had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue.
source: These differentially spliced exons include the AR-ESRP2-controlled alternative exons in the DOCK7 and RPS24 genes (both of which were excluded in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue); and the alternative exons in the MINK1 and MAP3K7 genes (each of which had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data

claim: MAP3K7 alternative exons had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue.
source: These differentially spliced exons include the AR-ESRP2-controlled alternative exons in the DOCK7 and RPS24 genes (both of which were excluded in prostate tumours compared to normal prostate tissue); and the alternative exons in the MINK1 and MAP3K7 genes (each of which had increased levels of splicing inclusion in prostate tumours compared to normal tissue).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA PRAD cohort data

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of an independent cohort confirmed more frequent skipping of DOCK7 exon 23 in prostate tumour tissue compared to normal prostate.
source: Further qRT-PCR analysis of an independent cohort confirmed more frequent skipping of DOCK7 (exon 23) and RPS24 (exon 5) in prostate tumour tissue compared to normal prostate (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of an independent cohort confirmed more frequent skipping of RPS24 exon 5 in prostate tumour tissue compared to normal prostate.
source: Further qRT-PCR analysis of an independent cohort confirmed more frequent skipping of DOCK7 (exon 23) and RPS24 (exon 5) in prostate tumour tissue compared to normal prostate (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Androgen induction of ESRP2 mRNA expression was blocked using the androgen antagonist bicalutamide (Casodex).
source: To test this, androgen induction of ESRP2 mRNA expression was blocked using the androgen antagonist bicalutamide (Casodex) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Casodex reduced the splicing inclusion of NUMB exon three.
source: Consistent with Casodex preventing expression of some potentially harmful isoforms in prostate cancer cells, the splicing inclusion of NUMB exon three and TUFT1 exon two were reduced by Casodex (both these exons are normally activated by androgen exposure and ESRP2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Casodex reduced the splicing inclusion of TUFT1 exon two.
source: Consistent with Casodex preventing expression of some potentially harmful isoforms in prostate cancer cells, the splicing inclusion of NUMB exon three and TUFT1 exon two were reduced by Casodex (both these exons are normally activated by androgen exposure and ESRP2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Exon skipping events in the RPS24, FN1 and MYH10 genes that correlated with a poorer prognosis were reduced by Casodex.
source: Likewise, exon skipping events in the RPS24, FN1 and MYH10 genes that correlated with a poorer prognosis were also reduced by Casodex (these exons are normally skipped in response to ESRP2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Skipping of CTNND1 exon 2 and 3 correlates with a decreased time to biochemical recurrence within the TGCA dataset.
source: Skipping of CTNND1 exon 2 and 3 correlates with a decreased time to biochemical recurrence within the TGCA dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and this is the mRNA isoform promoted by Casodex treatment (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Casodex treatment promotes the CTNND1 mRNA isoform with skipping of exons 2 and 3.
source: Skipping of CTNND1 exon 2 and 3 correlates with a decreased time to biochemical recurrence within the TGCA dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and this is the mRNA isoform promoted by Casodex treatment (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Casodex treatment increased splicing inclusion of MAGI1 exon 7.
source: Splicing inclusion of MAGI1 exon 7 (normally repressed by ESRP2) and RALGPS2 exon 15 were also increased by Casodex treatment (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Casodex treatment increased splicing inclusion of RALGPS2 exon 15.
source: Splicing inclusion of MAGI1 exon 7 (normally repressed by ESRP2) and RALGPS2 exon 15 were also increased by Casodex treatment (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Casodex treatment reduced splicing inclusion levels of FLNB gene exon 30 by almost 20%.
source: Consistent with this prediction, treatment of LNCaP cells with Casodex reduced splicing inclusion levels of the FLNB gene exon 30 by almost 20% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Increased skipping of FLNB exon 30 has been reported as a key driver of EMT in breast cancer development.
source: Although it is not differentially spliced between normal prostate and prostate cancer (Figure 5E), increased skipping of FLNB exon 30 has been recently reported as a key driver of EMT in breast cancer development (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation of Li et al., 2018

claim: Casodex treatment increased splicing inclusion of normally mesenchymal-expressed exons in the CTNND1 gene.
source: Similarly, Casodex treatment also increased splicing inclusion of what are normally mesenchymal-expressed exons in the CTNND1 gene (Warzecha et al., 2009b) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C and citation of Warzecha et al., 2009b

claim: ESRP2 protein expression was reduced by siRNA depletion of the AR.
source: As predicted, ESRP2 protein expression was reduced by siRNA depletion of the AR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of AR reduced levels of FLNB splicing inclusion from 84% to 69%.
source: Furthermore, siRNA-mediated depletion of AR reduced levels of FLNB splicing inclusion from 84% to 69%, and levels of TUFT1 exon 2 splicing from 23% to 9% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of AR reduced levels of TUFT1 exon 2 splicing from 23% to 9%.
source: Furthermore, siRNA-mediated depletion of AR reduced levels of FLNB splicing inclusion from 84% to 69%, and levels of TUFT1 exon 2 splicing from 23% to 9% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Single ESRP2 depletion was able to switch splicing patterns of exons within the MAP3K7, ARFGAP2 and CTNND1 genes.
source: Consistent with our model, single ESRP2 depletion was able to switch splicing patterns of exons within the MAP3K7, ARFGAP2 and CTNND1 genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Individual depletion of ESRP2 reduced splicing inclusion of MAP3K7 exon 12.
source: As examples, individual depletion of ESRP2 reduced splicing inclusion of MAP3K7 exon 12, and activated splicing inclusion of CTNND1 exons 2 and 3 (Figure 6 – Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Individual depletion of ESRP2 activated splicing inclusion of CTNND1 exons 2 and 3.
source: As examples, individual depletion of ESRP2 reduced splicing inclusion of MAP3K7 exon 12, and activated splicing inclusion of CTNND1 exons 2 and 3 (Figure 6 – Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Splicing patterns of ESRP1/ESRP2 target exons were responsive to single up-regulation of either ESRP1 or ESRP2.
source: Furthermore, splicing patterns of ESRP1/ESRP2 target exons were also responsive to single up-regulation of either ESRP1 or ESRP2 (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—source data 2

claim: The AR controls expression of the master splicing regulator protein ESRP2, which then regulates the splicing patterns of key genes important for prostate cancer biology.
source: In this model, the AR controls expression of the master splicing regulator protein ESRP2, which then regulates the splicing patterns of key genes important for prostate cancer biology (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary model based on the collective experimental findings

claim: ESRP2 is a direct and early target for transcriptional activation by the AR in prostate cancer cells.
source: Amongst the key data supporting this proposed model, we find that ESRP2 is a direct and early target for transcriptional activation by the AR in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing AR binding near ESRP2 and rapid induction of ESRP2 expression

claim: Endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 respond to androgen stimulation.
source: Furthermore, endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 also respond to androgen stimulation, siRNA-mediated depletion of the AR and/or the AR inhibitor bicalutamide (Casodex).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing splicing changes in response to these treatments

claim: Endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 respond to siRNA-mediated depletion of the AR.
source: Furthermore, endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 also respond to androgen stimulation, siRNA-mediated depletion of the AR and/or the AR inhibitor bicalutamide (Casodex).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing splicing changes after AR depletion

claim: Endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 respond to the AR inhibitor bicalutamide (Casodex).
source: Furthermore, endogenous splice isoform patterns controlled by ESRP1 and ESRP2 also respond to androgen stimulation, siRNA-mediated depletion of the AR and/or the AR inhibitor bicalutamide (Casodex).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing splicing changes after Casodex treatment

claim: ADT utilises drugs to inhibit gonadal and extra-gonadal androgen biosynthesis and competitive AR antagonists to block androgen binding and abrogate AR function.
source: ADT utilises drugs to inhibit gonadal and extra-gonadal androgen biosynthesis and competitive AR antagonists to block androgen binding and abrogate AR function (Livermore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation

claim: After 2–3 years of ADT, tumours often grow again, developing castration resistance with a median survival time of 16 months.
source: ADT delays disease progression, but after 2–3 years tumours often grow again, developing castration resistance with a median survival time of 16 months (Karantanos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation

claim: The process of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) plays a pivotal role in prostate cancer metastasis.
source: The process of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) plays a pivotal role in prostate cancer metastasis (Gravdal et al., 2007; Matuszak and Kyprianou, 2011; Min et al., 2010; Saini et al., 2011; Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations

claim: ADT has been shown to directly induce EMT in both mouse and human prostate tissue.
source: While the mechanisms driving EMT in prostate cancer are poorly understood, ADT has recently been shown to directly induce EMT in both mouse and human prostate tissue (Sun et al., 2012; Zhifang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Sun et al., 2012 and Zhifang et al., 2015

claim: Changes in alternative splicing patterns can have dramatic effects on EMT and on metastatic disease progression.
source: Importantly, changes in alternative splicing patterns can have dramatic effects on EMT and on metastatic disease progression (Pradella et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pradella et al., 2017

claim: ESRP1 and ESRP2 are important regulators of epithelial alternative splicing patterns.
source: ESRP2 and its close relative ESRP1 (60% identical to ESRP2 protein) are important regulators of epithelial alternative splicing patterns (Bebee et al., 2015; Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009; Oltean and Bates, 2014; Valastyan and Weinberg, 2011; Warzecha et al., 2010; Warzecha et al., 2009a; Warzecha et al., 2009b), reduced expression of which can drive critical aspects of EMT (Hayakawa et al., 2017; Pradella et al., 2017; Warzecha et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations

claim: Reduced expression of ESRP1 and ESRP2 can drive critical aspects of EMT.
